title: The WAVES open to Black women
photoNote: Harriet Ida Pickens and Frances Wills after graduating from the Naval Reserve Midshipmen's School, Northampton, Massachusetts, December 1944. U.S. Navy photo 80-G-297441 (NARA), public domain. Taken about two months after the 19 October announcement.
body:
For more than two years, the Navy's women's reserve had turned away Black women. On this day that changed.

19 October 1944. With President Roosevelt's approval, the Navy announced that African American women could join the WAVES.

Two of them made history fast. Harriet Ida Pickens and Frances Wills trained at the Naval Reserve Midshipmen's School on the Smith College campus in Northampton, Massachusetts. On 26 December 1944 they were commissioned as the Navy's first Black women officers.

This photo shows them that December, packing up after graduation. Two days later, the first Black enlisted WAVES reported for training at Hunter College in New York.

For more than two years, the Navy's women's reserve turned away Black women.

19 October 1944. With President Roosevelt's approval, the Navy announced that African American women could join the WAVES.

That December, Harriet Ida Pickens and Frances Wills became the Navy's first Black women officers.

declassified.fact: Harriet Pickens already knew the campus where she trained. She was a Smith College graduate, one of six in her class to finish with highest honors, and the midshipmen's school sat on Smith's grounds. Her father, William Pickens, was an early NAACP leader who lobbied for Black women in the Navy and recommended her for the WAVES.
